name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,623

clue.text: Perhaps Blair years ultimately written about as corrupt

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: Tony Blair was Prime Minister for about ten years, 1997 to 2007; 'perhaps' marks this as one example of the span
the final letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A political jibe that the Blair government years were rotten and corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' governs both 'written' and 'about', taking the tail of each.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent describes moral decline and self-indulgence, a close synonym of morally rotten or debased.

clue.text: Those last seen in militia will attack Area 51 base

indicators.note: the letters seen last in a run of words are their final letters, so each word gives up its tail

blocks.note: the final letters of these four words
51 in Roman numerals is L (50) plus I (1)

explanation.surface: Armed militia plan to storm Area 51, the secret US military base in Nevada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like part of the military installation's name but is the chemistry definition; the number is read as Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry an alkali is a soluble base, one that neutralises acids, so the two terms overlap closely.

clue.text: Deceptive designs sending a PC to trial

indicators.note: to send someone is to transport or carry them away, so these letters are sent into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Deceitful schemes send a police constable to face trial, perhaps as a frame-up.
explanation.walkthrough: PC here is a police constable in the surface; its letters just join the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Optical art, or op art, uses patterns that trick the eye into seeing movement, so its designs deceive the viewer.

clue.text: Federal investigators over the pond uncovered something in the water

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters are taken off both ends

blocks.note: the FBI is the Federal Bureau of Investigation in America, across the Atlantic

explanation.surface: American federal agents discover something lurking in the water supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the pond' means in America; 'water' is a polite word for urine, not the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Urea is the main nitrogen compound excreted in urine, so it is literally found in passed water.

clue.text: Operation's legal proceedings repeatedly failing to get answers

indicators.note: failing to get something means going without it, and doing so repeatedly means every instance is dropped

blocks.note: a case and an action are both lawsuits
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: An operation's court cases keep collapsing without any answers.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'proceedings' supplies two separate words for a lawsuit; each loses its A. The apostrophe-s is read as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A caesarean section is a surgical operation delivering a baby through an incision in the abdomen.

clue.text: At least 100 coppers or plods

blocks.note: first meaning: sums of a hundred pence or more, coppers being copper coins
second meaning: walks heavily

explanation.surface: A count of a hundred or more police officers, or plods, as Britons call them.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'coppers' and 'plods' are British slang for police; here coppers are pennies and plods is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pound is worth one hundred pence, and to pound is to tread with heavy, laborious steps.

clue.text: Snatch of metal caught on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard rather than seen, so the word is judged only by its sound

blocks.note: steel is an alloy, a metal

explanation.surface: A brief fragment of heavy metal music heard on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snatch' suggests a short excerpt of music but is the verb meaning to take.
explanation.definitionFit: To snatch something is to grab it quickly, which is a way to take it unlawfully, a synonym.

clue.text: Friendly note on beauty treatment has lowered tone

indicators.note: to lower something can mean to let it drop, so a part is dropped out of the word

blocks.note: so (or soh) is the fifth note of the sol-fa scale
a facial is a skincare treatment for the face
fa is another sol-fa note

explanation.surface: A sociable salon note explaining that a beauty treatment has a softer tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just places one piece before the other in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Social describes someone who enjoys company and mixing with others, a close match for friendly or sociable.

clue.text: Bent coppers i.e. people in deep may be shown up by this

definitions.text: people in deep may be shown up by this

indicators.note: something bent is twisted out of shape, so these letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Corrupt police officers, deep in their crimes, can be exposed by this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent coppers' is British slang for corrupt police; 'deep' is the sea, and 'shown up' means raised to the surface view.
explanation.definitionFit: Submariners deep underwater raise a periscope to look above the surface, so it shows things up to them.

clue.text: Preview clip with culprit finally sent down ...  this calls for a celebration

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the word is used
in a down entry, sending something down moves it lower, here into a slot further down the word

blocks.note: a teaser is a short trailer; the culprit's letter is lifted out of its front
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A trailer showing the guilty party being jailed is something worth celebrating.
explanation.walkthrough: TEASER is the preview; its opening T, which is the culprit's last letter, moves down three places. 'Sent down' also means jailed in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the Christian festival marking the resurrection, a major annual feast and holiday.

clue.text: Fella briefly engaged in dodgy activity to make some bread

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, so the final letter is clipped

blocks.note: a chap is a man, a fella
to be 'at it' is British slang for being up to no good

explanation.surface: A man briefly turned to crime to earn some money, bread being slang for cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks attached to 'Fella' but trims the phrase that follows. 'Bread' meaning money is the surface sense; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is a flat unleavened Indian bread cooked on a griddle, an example of a bread.

clue.text: AC-12's coppers showing signs of stress

blocks.note: the unit's letters, without its number
cents are small copper coins

explanation.surface: The anti-corruption officers of AC-12, the unit in Line of Duty, are showing strain.
explanation.walkthrough: AC-12 is the police anti-corruption unit in the BBC drama; only its letters are used, and 'coppers' are coins, not police.
explanation.definitionFit: Accent marks written over vowels show where a word's stress falls, so they are signs of emphasis in pronunciation.

clue.text: Country's crime data evenly distributed

indicators.note: evenly picks the letters in even-numbered positions of the word just before
distributed means spread around, so the letters are spread into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A nation's crime statistics are spread evenly across its regions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evenly distributed' reads as one phrase, but 'evenly' works on 'data' and 'distributed' mixes everything.
explanation.definitionFit: America is commonly used for the United States, a nation, so it is a straightforward example of a country.

clue.text: Report from snout reportedly being discussed

indicators.note: what is passed on by word of mouth is heard, not read, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a sneeze is the noise a nose makes; snout is slang for nose

explanation.surface: An informant's report, snout being British slang for a police informer, is being debated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snout' looks like the police informer but is a nose, and its report is a sneeze; atishoo is the British spelling of achoo.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter at issue is the point in dispute, the topic currently under debate or consideration.

clue.text: Isn't it arch working for the enemy?

indicators.note: working means being worked or kneaded into shape, so these letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wry question: is it not rather knowing to be a double agent working for the other side?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' means knowing or sly in the surface; here it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In Christian belief the Antichrist is the great adversary of Christ, the ultimate foe of the faithful.

clue.text: Police leader probing strange deaths

indicators.note: strange means odd or unfamiliar, so the letters are made unfamiliar by rearranging
to probe is to push inside something, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: Sting was lead singer of the band The Police
taken as written

explanation.surface: A senior police officer investigates a series of suspicious deaths.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines Superintendent Ted Hastings, head of AC-12 in the BBC drama Line of Duty, while the wordplay reads 'Police' as the rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: Ted Hastings leads the anti-corruption unit in Line of Duty and is regularly shown investigating suspicious killings.

clue.text: Fancy riding in gear some time?

blocks.note: gear is clothing, dress
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Would you like to go riding in your kit at some point?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like a verb inviting someone but is an adjective for elaborate.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the competitive equestrian discipline of precise, elegant trained movements, an elaborate style of horsemanship.

clue.text: Isolated police officers brought back to catch wicked one

indicators.note: to bring something back is to return it the way it came, so the letters run the other way
catching something means holding it inside, so one piece closes around another

blocks.note: cops are police officers
wicked and rad are both slang for excellent
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Lone officers are recalled to arrest an evil person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' means evil in the surface but is youth slang for great.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring here and there or now and then, scattered like separate isolated instances.

clue.text: New recruit covering up corruption?

blocks.note: a cover-up denies, saying there is none
vice is depravity, corruption

explanation.surface: A fresh police recruit is helping to hide wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the loose idea that covering up corruption amounts to declaring there is none.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice is a beginner or newcomer, someone just taken on and inexperienced, which fits a fresh entrant.

clue.text: Superintendent sets example, arresting sucker

indicators.note: to arrest is to hold in custody, so the words hold the answer within them

blocks.note: the letters sit across the end of the first word, the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A police superintendent leads by example by arresting a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' suggests a gullible dupe, but it is an insect that sucks blood.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse is an African fly that feeds by sucking the blood of animals and people, so it is literally a bloodsucker.

clue.text: Most smooth, detailed poet from the east has India at heart

indicators.note: detailed read as de-tailed means having its tail cut off, so the last letter goes
in an across clue reading from the east means right to left, the reverse of normal
to have something is to hold it, so one piece contains the other
at the heart means in the very middle, which is where the insertion is placed

blocks.note: T S Eliot, the poet, without his final letter
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A suave, elaborately described poet from the Orient has a love of India at his core.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'in detail' but means de-tailed. The poet is T S Eliot, including his initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Oily describes an unctuous, ingratiating smoothness of manner, so the superlative means the smoothest of all.

clue.text: Criminal due to fly in for police show featuring 14

indicators.note: criminal means crooked or bent, so these letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A criminal is set to be flown in for an episode of a police drama starring the 14 character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal. 14 refers to the answer to 14 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: Line of Duty is the BBC police drama about anti-corruption unit AC-12, in which Ted Hastings is the central superintendent.

clue.text: Copper's bringing posh Spanish banker in for questioning

indicators.note: bringing something in means taking it inside, so the other pieces go within

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper, plus the possessive S
a banker is a river, which has banks, and rio is Spanish for river
U means upper-class

explanation.surface: A police officer brings in an upper-class Spanish banker to be interviewed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is the element, not a policeman, and 'banker' is a river rather than a financier.
explanation.definitionFit: Curious means inquisitive and eager to find things out, the same sense as an inquiring or questioning mind.

clue.text: Worker in community armed DS Arnott regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Detective Sergeant Steve Arnott of Line of Duty, armed, often works in the community.
explanation.walkthrough: DS Arnott is a lead character in the BBC series; 'community' is an ant colony.
explanation.definitionFit: Red ants live in colonies where most members are workers, so one is a labourer in an insect society.

clue.text: Acclaimed, but first to be dismissed and charged

indicators.note: dismissing the first means sending away the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: lionised means celebrated, made much of

explanation.surface: A celebrated officer, but the first to be sacked and prosecuted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' suggests a criminal charge but is electrical.
explanation.definitionFit: An ionised atom has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electric charge.

clue.text: See 20
Beaming traitor keeps lead from DI Fleming?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds the others inside
the lead of something is its front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: a rat is a betrayer
the first letter
Ian Fleming created James Bond

explanation.surface: A smiling traitor holds the lead in DI Kate Fleming's Line of Duty case.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: the Fleming here is not DI Kate Fleming from the drama but the Bond author.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiant can mean glowing with happiness, so a radiant face is beaming with joy.

clue.text: After coupling with another, tech billionaire stretches

blocks.note: Elon Musk, another tech billionaire
Bill Gates, founder of Microsoft

explanation.surface: A tech billionaire grows his empire after a merger with another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After coupling with' tells you the billionaire comes second, joined to another of the same kind.
explanation.definitionFit: To elongate something is to make it longer, which is what stretching it does, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Innocent Methuselah framed by villain on tape

indicators.note: a tape recording is played back and heard, so the word counts only for its sound
a frame surrounds a picture, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a knave is a rogue
the setter's pseudonym, standing for me

explanation.surface: The setter claims innocence, framed by a crook caught on a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves by their own pseudonym; here it gives the first-person pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive means artless and lacking worldly experience, an innocent in the sense of guileless.
